title: IB Economics Exam Technique for November
summary: IB Economics exam technique for November: master each paper, manage timing, use evidence effectively and build a focused three-week revision plan.
body_markdown:
Effective **IB Economics exam technique** means knowing what each paper rewards, allocating time according to marks, and practising decisions under pressure. In the final three weeks before November, focus on choosing questions, explaining diagrams, applying evidence and finishing responses.


That period can feel compressed. There is enough time to improve, but little value in rereading everything without testing what you can produce. The practical task is to turn workable knowledge into clear, complete answers.


### The November exam checklist


Before timed practice, confirm that you can:


- respond precisely to command terms
- draw and explain core diagrams
- develop real-world examples for Paper 1
- integrate stimulus evidence into Paper 2
- complete calculations and recommendations for HL Paper 3
- finish within the official time


Paper Who sits it? Time Maximum marks Main task


Paper 1 SL and HL 1 hour 15 minutes 25 Answer one extended-response question from three choices


Paper 2 SL and HL 1 hour 45 minutes 40 Answer one data-response question from two choices


Paper 3 HL only 1 hour 45 minutes 60 Answer both quantitative and policy questions


Paper 1 contributes 30% at SL and 20% at HL. Paper 2 contributes 40% at SL and 30% at HL. Paper 3 contributes 30% at HL. See[IB Economics Paper 1 vs Paper 2](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-economics-paper-1-vs-paper-2) for a broader comparison.


### Week three: make Paper 1 predictable


Paper 1 offers three questions. You answer one, comprising a 10-mark part (a) and a 15-mark part (b).


Read all three before choosing. Underline command terms and test each option: Do I know the theory? Can I explain the relevant diagram? Do I have a developed real-world example?


Choose by the demands of both parts. A familiar opening question can conceal a more difficult evaluation task.


### Build the 10-mark explanation


Define the central term, establish the economic mechanism and explain its consequences in sequence. Include an accurately labelled diagram where appropriate, then connect it explicitly to the question.


Label axes, curves, equilibria and relevant areas. Explain what changes and why. A diagram left unexplained leaves the reader to reconstruct your reasoning.


### Develop the 15-mark judgement


Part (b) requires relevant theory, application and evaluation. Develop benefits and limitations using conditions such as time, stakeholder effects, elasticity and the state of the economy.


Attach evaluation to the argument it qualifies. For example, judging a minimum wage requires considering its level, labour-demand elasticity, enforcement and market conditions.


Prepare a small bank of examples you understand well. For each, record the country, policy or event, relevant economic mechanism and a limitation. Avoid memorising unsupported numbers. An example earns its place when you explain how its details support or qualify your argument.


Try roughly 25-30 minutes for part (a) and 40-45 minutes for part (b), including planning and checking. These are practice allocations, not official rules. Refine your approach with[RevisionDojo’s guide to long Economics questions](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-economics-how-to-answer-long-questions) .

### Week two: extract Paper 2 marks


Paper 2 asks you to complete one of two data-response questions. Its shorter parts have question-specific requirements; the final 15-mark response uses a markband.


Read the questions before annotating the stimulus. Identify relevant definitions, changes, stakeholders, policies and numbers. This gives your reading a purpose.


For definitions, state the precise economic meaning. For calculations, write the formula, substitute values, show working and include units. Visible working may demonstrate a valid method even when the final result is incorrect.


For explanations, match depth to marks and apply the mechanism to the context. If the stimulus describes falling production costs, connect that evidence to the relevant supply change and explain the resulting effects.


The final response needs theory, accurate application and evaluation. Use several specific stimulus references throughout. A useful sequence is claim, theory, evidence, implication and evaluation. Develop a contrasting argument, then make a qualified judgement.


When using a figure, identify what it measures and the period it covers. Distinguish a percentage change from a percentage-point change. If two indicators move together, explain the proposed economic connection rather than assuming that one caused the other. These checks keep application precise.


During practice, aim to protect approximately 40 minutes for this response. Adjust using your completion times. The[IB Economics exam tips guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-economics-exam-tips) offers further support.


### Week one for HL: connect calculations to policy


Paper 3 contains two compulsory 30-mark questions. Each has shorter analytical and quantitative tasks worth 20 marks in total, followed by a 10-mark recommendation.


Calculators are permitted, but interpretation still matters. Show formulas and working, then explain the economic meaning where required. An elasticity value becomes useful when connected to responsiveness, revenue, tax incidence or policy effectiveness.


For each recommendation, identify the problem, propose a clear policy and use supplied evidence. Explain the mechanism, consider constraints and stakeholder effects, then justify your judgement.


Start with about 50 minutes per question and five minutes for checking. Protect recommendation time so calculations do not consume the paper.


### The final three days: review what costs marks


Use the[IB Economics Questionbank](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-economics/questionbank) for targeted practice, then complete timed sessions with[Test Builder and Exam Mode](https://www.revisiondojo.com/features/test-builder) .


Classify lost marks by cause: knowledge gaps, weak application, missing diagram labels, undeveloped evaluation, calculation errors or unfinished responses. Select the next exercise from that diagnosis.


Keep an error log with three entries: the mistake, the correction and a question that tests the correction. Reattempt that question without your notes the following day. This makes review concrete and shows whether the repair survives independent practice.


RevisionDojo’s Study Notes and Flashcards can support knowledge repair. AI Chat and Grading tools can help you examine explanations, while Predicted Papers and Mock Exams support timing practice. The Coursework Library provides examples to examine, and Tutors offer another route to conceptual support.


Use[topic-by-topic Economics revision](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-economics-topic-by-topic-revision) to address gaps, then return to timed writing. Check that feedback matches your teacher’s guidance and the relevant assessment criteria.


### Walk into November with a repeatable process


Choose questions carefully, allocate time by marks, explain diagrams and make evaluation conditional. Practise these decisions until they feel familiar. RevisionDojo brings preparation and review together, helping you spend the final weeks correcting specific weaknesses and keeping your attention on the economics.
